summary: Specifies a Telnet option that lets a terminal session work one line at a time instead of one character at a time. The client edits the line locally and sends it when finished, which cuts network traffic and delays. It is a standards-track document that obsoletes RFC 1116.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing each letter separately, you write the whole sentence and mail it once. That is faster and uses fewer envelopes.

questions: how does telnet send a line at a time
what does the telnet slc suboption do
why does telnet send one line at a time
subtitle: Lets a Telnet client edit a command line locally and send it only when it is done, instead of one packet per keystroke.

tldr.problem: Character-at-a-time Telnet makes echo slow over long-delay networks, burdens machines that handle single characters poorly, and cannot express many special characters cleanly.
tldr.mechanism: The LINEMODE option (code 34) negotiates a mode with EDIT and TRAPSIG bits, a table of special characters (SLC) the client agrees on with the server, and an optional forward mask that says when buffered input is sent.
tldr.outcome: Network traffic drops to a couple of packets per command line. It is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1116, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes it.

today: RFC 1184 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1116, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Linemode Telnet Is
sections.content:
Linemode Telnet does terminal character processing on the client side of a Telnet connection. With editing enabled locally, network traffic falls to a couple of packets per command line, rather than a couple of packets per character typed.

This helps on long delay networks, because the user gets local response while typing and pays the network delay only once the line is sent. It also helps on networks that charge per packet.

This RFC obsoletes RFC 1116. It adds two mode bits, SOFT_TAB and LIT_ECHO, which advise the client how to echo tabs and non-printable characters, and several new special character mappings for cursor motion in visual editing.
sections.eli5: Instead of phoning a friend after every letter you type, you finish your whole sentence and then make one call.

sections.title: Why a New Option Was Needed
sections.content:
The RFC gives two reasons. First, over long delay equipment it is frustrating when echoing a user's typing takes several seconds. Second, some supercomputers are poor at single-character input, so it is better for a front end to do the character processing and leave the supercomputer's cycles for number crunching.

Earlier attempts at local line editing within existing Telnet leaned on the state of the ECHO and SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD options. Using ECHO alone gives no way to turn echo off while keeping local processing on, for example while typing a password. Reading SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD as 'line at a time' is, in the RFC's words, not what that option is supposed to mean. Telnet also lacked enough special characters, so implementations borrowed the BRK option for a second interrupt and the EOR option for end-of-file. Some line modes buffered a whole line and sent it with editing characters still in it.

The conclusion was to define new options that support local line editing in a reasonable, reliable and consistent way.
sections.eli5: The old tricks were like using a spoon as a screwdriver. They sort of worked, but a proper tool was needed.

sections.title: Editing and Signal Trapping
sections.content:
Two ideas define the states of interest. Local line editing means normal command line processing such as Erase Character and Erase Line happens on the local system, and the edited data goes to the remote system only when CR LF or some other special character is typed. Signal trapping means that typing the character for a function like IP sends IAC IP instead of the typed character. Remote signal trapping does the opposite: the actual character is sent.

That gives three interesting combinations: local editing with local trapping, remote editing with local trapping, and remote editing with remote trapping. Local editing with remote trapping is not interesting, because the client would not recognize signals and special signals usually affect the line editing function.
sections.eli5: Editing is fixing your homework before handing it in. Trapping is the teacher's special words, like 'stop', being understood on your side instead of being passed along as letters.

sections.title: Negotiating the Mode
sections.content:
The option is LINEMODE, code 34, and its default is WONT/DONT, meaning no sub-negotiation of the connection mode. The client side sends WILL LINEMODE and the server side sends DO LINEMODE. DO LINEMODE must never be negotiated in both directions: the side that sent DO is the server and the side that sent WILL is the client.

The MODE suboption (code 1) carries a bit mask. EDIT (1) makes the client process input lines and send only completed lines. TRAPSIG (2) makes the client translate interrupts such as IP, BRK, AYT, ABORT, EOF and SUSP into their Telnet equivalents. MODE_ACK (4) marks a confirmation. SOFT_TAB (8) asks the client to expand tabs into spaces, and LIT_ECHO (16) asks it to echo non-printable characters literally. Flow control and echo logically belong in the mask but use the existing TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL and ECHO options instead; the client must never negotiate WILL ECHO.

Normally the server starts mode changes and the client confirms them. A client MUST agree with at least the EDIT and TRAPSIG bits. A MODE identical to the current one is ignored, and a MODE with MODE_ACK set never gets a reply, so both sides settle on the same mode.
sections.eli5: The two computers agree on a few switches, like 'edit here' and 'catch the stop key here', and each switch flip gets a thumbs-up.

sections.title: Special Characters (SLC)
sections.content:
The SLC suboption (code 3) carries lists of three octets: the function, modifiers, and the ASCII character. A function can be at one of four levels, from highest to lowest: SLC_DEFAULT, SLC_VALUE, SLC_CANTCHANGE and SLC_NOSUPPORT. The modifier octet can also carry SLC_ACK (128), SLC_FLUSHIN (64) and SLC_FLUSHOUT (32).

Functions fall in two groups. Some map to Telnet equivalents, such as SYNCH, BRK, IP, AO, AYT, EOR, ABORT, EOF and SUSP. Others are handled locally, such as Erase Character, Erase Line, Erase Word, Reprint Line, Literal Next, XON, XOFF, two forwarding characters and the cursor-motion and visual-edit functions. The three new control characters are IAC ABORT, IAC SUSP and IAC EOF.

When a connection starts, the client must either send its own special characters or ask for the server's by sending SLC 0 SLC_DEFAULT 0. The client is in control of the settings. A receiver ignores a request equal to its current setting, acknowledges one it agrees with by setting SLC_ACK, and may disagree only by answering with a different value at a lower level. If both sides ask to change the same character, they settle on the client's value.
sections.eli5: It is a list that says which key means 'erase a letter', which means 'erase the line', and so on. The user's computer gets to decide, and the other side says yes or suggests a smaller change.

sections.title: Forwarding and Flushing
sections.content:
The server can say when the client should send its buffered input. SLC_FORW1 and SLC_FORW2 name up to two extra forwarding characters, while the FORWARDMASK suboption (code 2) sends a mask of up to 32 octets, one bit per ASCII code. If the mask ends early, the remaining octets count as zero, and an octet equal to IAC must be doubled. The client must forward on those characters, on any normal line terminator and on any special signal. It may forward more often, but in EDIT mode should avoid doing so at random because the forwarded part can no longer be edited.

For IP, BRK or ABORT, SLC_FLUSHIN and SLC_FLUSHOUT are advisory bits asking for the input stream and pending output to be flushed. The standard method uses the Telnet Synch signal for input and the TIMING-MARK option for output: the sender sends IAC XXX IAC DM IAC DO TIMING-MARK. The DM is sent as TCP urgent data. Whenever an IAC AO arrives, a Synch must be returned.

Output processing is always the server's job, whichever mode is in effect: CR LF for a newline, CR NUL for just a carriage return and LF for just a linefeed. In EDIT mode the client sends CR LF as the line terminator.
sections.eli5: The client holds your words until it sees a signal like a full stop, and then sends them all at once.

sections.title: A Sample Connection
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a whole session. The server sends DO TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL and DO LINEMODE, the client answers with WILL for both and sends its list of special characters, and the server sets the initial mode to EDIT and acknowledges them.

At the password prompt the server sends WILL ECHO, which stops the client echoing, and then WONT ECHO afterwards. When an application wants single-character mode with its own echoing but still wants signals trapped, the server sets the mode to TRAPSIG. An application that wants full control sets mode 0.

The final example has an editor ask for forwarding only on control characters, which is done with DO FORWARDMASK, and then restore EDIT|TRAPSIG and DONT FORWARDMASK once the application ends.
sections.eli5: It shows the computers trading notes about the rules, then changing the rules when you type a password or start a program.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not discuss security. Its Security Considerations section consists of a single sentence saying that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: The authors did not write anything about safety in this document.
